back: An organism too small to be seen clearly without a microscope, e.g. a bacterium, a yeast or a mould.
notes: Viruses are studied with them, though they are not cells.

back: Genetic material (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat. No membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes or nucleus: not a cell.
Only inside living host cells: the host cell is made to build new viruses, which are released, often killing the cell.

front: Name the parts of a bacterial cell.
back: Cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, a loop of DNA (no nucleus), plasmids; sometimes a flagellum or capsule.
Asexual reproduction in which one cell divides into two identical cells: how bacteria reproduce.
notes: In ideal conditions some bacteria divide every 20 minutes.

back: Cells with nuclei and chitin walls; no chlorophyll; made of hyphae forming a mycelium (yeast is single-celled); reproduce by spores.
An organism that feeds on dead organic matter by secreting enzymes onto it and absorbing the soluble products.
notes: Most fungi and many bacteria are saprotrophs (decomposers).

front: How do yeast and bread mould reproduce?
back: Yeast: budding. Bread mould: spores released from black spore cases (sporangia).
Decomposition (recycling); bioremediation; nitrogen fixation; food and drink (bread, beer, sour milk, yoghurt, cheese); medicines (penicillin, insulin).

front: Give examples of harm done by microorganisms.
back: Disease: cholera, TB (bacteria); HIV, measles (viruses); ringworm (fungus); maize streak, rusts, foot-and-mouth. Food spoilage and toxins, e.g. aflatoxins.

front: What is the principle behind food preservation?
back: Remove what microorganisms need (water, warmth) or kill them: drying, refrigeration, salting, sugar, vinegar, boiling, pasteurising, canning.
